The null coalescing operator (??) is equivalent to isset() checks and suppresses warnings for undefined variables or array keys.
echo can take multiple comma-separated arguments, so it outputs 'a' followed by 'b'.
In PHP, print is a language construct that always returns 1, so it can be used within expressions, unlike echo which returns no value.
The elvis operator ($a ?: $b) returns the left operand when it is truthy, and the right operand only when the left is falsy.
PHP 8 lowered the precedence of the concatenation operator so that '+' and '-' are evaluated before '.', e.g. 1 + 2 . '3' now yields '33' instead of '13'.
The ** operator is right-associative in PHP, so 2 ** 3 ** 2 equals 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 512.
In PHP 8, '.' and '+' have equal precedence and are left-associative, so ('sum: ' . 2) + 3 attempts to add a non-numeric string and throws a fatal TypeError.
With ===, arrays must have the same key/value pairs in the same order with identical types to be equal.
0 == false uses loose comparison and returns true; strict comparison would require the === operator.
Since PHP 8, comparing a non-numeric string to a number casts the number to a string, so "abc" == 0 is false (it was true in PHP 7).
With loose comparison in PHP, null == 0, null == '', and null == false all evaluate to true.
Casting a string to int reads the leading numeric portion and stops at the first non-numeric character.
PHP converts the numeric string '5' to an integer, so the addition yields 10.
In PHP, casting false to string yields an empty string "", while true becomes "1".
Due to floating-point precision, 0.1 + 0.2 equals 0.30000000000000004, which is not strictly identical to 0.3.
strrev() reverses a string byte-by-byte, which corrupts multibyte UTF-8 characters instead of correctly reversing them.
str_contains() returns true when the haystack contains the needle, and 'world' appears in 'Hello world' (PHP 8+).
str_pad() can pad on the right, left, or both sides via its optional pad_type argument (STR_PAD_RIGHT, STR_PAD_LEFT, STR_PAD_BOTH).
By default trim() strips whitespace characters including spaces, tabs, newlines, carriage returns, null bytes, and vertical tabs.
strlen() counts bytes, and 'é' occupies 2 bytes in UTF-8, so 'héllo' is 6 bytes.
A negative start of -3 counts from the end of the string, so it returns the last three characters 'def'.
PHP strings are immutable and ucfirst() returns a new string rather than modifying the argument in place.

sort() reindexes the array with numeric keys starting at 0, so it does not preserve key-value associations (asort() does).
PHP automatically casts array keys that are canonical decimal integer strings (like '5') to integers.
in_array() uses loose comparison (==) by default; strict comparison is enabled only when the third parameter is set to true.
When called without a callback, array_filter() keeps only elements that evaluate to true (removing falsy values like 0, '', null, false, and '0').
array_slice() reindexes numeric keys by default; you must pass true as the fourth argument (preserve_keys) to keep them.
array_slice starts at offset 1 (element 20) and takes 2 elements, returning [20, 30].
The + union operator keeps keys from the left array when they collide, so the result is ['a' => 1, 'b' => 2], which has 2 elements.
PHP 8.1 added support for unpacking arrays with string keys using the spread operator in array literals.
Since PHP 8.1, argument unpacking can pass named arguments by using an array with string keys, so the two can be combined in a single call.
In PHP, anonymous functions do not inherit outer scope variables automatically; they must be imported explicitly with the use clause (or arrow functions, which do capture automatically).
func_num_args() returns the actual number of arguments passed to the function at call time, regardless of the declared parameter list.
PHP arrow functions (fn) can only contain a single expression, not multiple statements in curly braces.
Arrow functions automatically capture outer variables by value (at definition time), not by reference; only anonymous functions with an explicit use(&$var) capture by reference.
A static closure cannot bind $this automatically or manually, so $this is not available inside it.
The closure captures $x by value at the time of creation, so later changes to $x do not affect it.
In weak typing mode, PHP coerces numeric strings like "5" to int for int-typed parameters.
Constructor property promotion was introduced in PHP 8.0, allowing visibility modifiers directly in constructor parameters.
The `final` keyword on a method prevents subclasses from overriding it.
The final keyword prevents a method from being overridden by child classes.
Private properties of a parent class are not accessible in a subclass; only protected and public ones are.
An anonymous class is named class@anonymous, followed by a NUL byte, the file path, and line number.
Private methods are not inherited or overridden, so a child class may declare a same-named method with any visibility without violating inheritance rules.
__get() is called for inaccessible properties as well, meaning private or protected properties accessed from outside their scope, not just non-existent ones.
In PHP, modifying a readonly property after initialization throws an instance of Error, not Exception.
PHP interfaces may define constants that implementing classes inherit.
The instanceof operator determines whether an object is an instance of a class, an interface, or an inherited class.
PHP interfaces may declare static methods, which implementing classes must define as static with a compatible signature.
The instanceof operator also returns true if the object implements a given interface, not just for class inheritance.
In PHP, interface methods cannot contain a body/default implementation; that capability belongs to traits (and classes), unlike some other languages such as Java.
In PHP, abstract methods may be declared public, protected, or (since PHP 7.1) private, so protected visibility is allowed.
cases() returns an array of all enum cases, and Foo defines three: A, B, and C.
Since PHP 8.2, traits can declare constants, which are then inherited by classes using the trait (before that it was not allowed).
In PHP 7+, both Exception and Error implement the Throwable interface, making it their common ancestor.
TypeError extends Error, not Exception; both only share the Throwable interface, so catch (Exception) does not catch TypeError.
The @ operator only suppresses error diagnostics (like warnings and notices); exceptions are still thrown and must be caught.
intdiv() throws a DivisionByZeroError (an ArithmeticError subclass) when the divisor is zero.
The finally block always runs after try, whether or not an exception was thrown or caught.
An exception thrown inside a finally block overrides (discards) any return value or pending exception from the try block, so it directly affects the result.
Casting any object (including an Exception instance) to bool in PHP always yields true.
Shutdown functions registered with register_shutdown_function() are executed after script termination, including when exit() or die() is called or a fatal error occurs.
The use statement only creates an alias; the class file is loaded only when the class is actually used (e.g., instantiated), typically via autoloading.
In PHP, namespaced functions are imported with 'use function', while constants use 'use const'.
The App\ prefix is stripped and the remaining namespace maps to directories, so UserController goes to src/Controller/Api/UserController.php.
Composer's generated vendor/autoload.php registers autoloader functions through spl_autoload_register().
__NAMESPACE__ is a magic constant that holds the name of the current namespace (empty string in global scope).

An unqualified class name in `new` is resolved relative to the current namespace (with import aliases applied), not from the global root; only fully qualified names with a leading \ refer to the global root.
PSR-4 replaces the namespace prefix 'App\' with the base directory 'src/', so App\Model\User maps to src/Model/User.php.
use statements are only allowed in the outermost scope of a file or within a namespace block; they apply to the whole file, not to individual functions.
In PHP, arrays use value semantics with copy-on-write, so assigning an array to another variable creates a copy unless you explicitly reference it with &.
PHP arrays are copied by value, so modifying $b does not affect $a, which still has 2 elements.
PHP functions have their own local scope, so global variables are not visible inside a function unless imported via the global keyword, accessed through $GLOBALS, or passed as arguments.
Unsetting $GLOBALS['x'] removes the global variable itself at the superglobal level, affecting all scopes, not just the current function.
The parameter is passed by reference, so incrementing $x modifies $n directly.
A foreach by value iterates over a snapshot (copy) of the array, so modifications made inside the loop do not affect the elements visited in the current pass.
Static properties belong to the class itself and are shared across all instances, so a change made via one object is visible in all others.
PHP casts boolean array keys to integers, so true is stored as the integer key 1, not as a bool.
Since PHP 7.0, a generator's return expression can be retrieved by calling getReturn() on the generator object after it finishes.
Generators are forward-only iterators; calling rewind() on a started generator throws an exception.
`yield from` delegates iteration to another generator, Traversable object, or array.
Calling a generator function returns a Generator object, so get_class returns the class name 'Generator'.
The generator yields three values (1, 2, 3) via `yield from`, so `iterator_to_array` produces an array of 3 elements.
SplStack implements a LIFO stack (last-in, first-out), not a FIFO queue; SplQueue is the FIFO implementation.
ArrayIterator wraps an array (or object) and implements the Iterator interface, enabling traversal with standard iterator methods like rewind(), current(), and next().
ArrayObject implements IteratorAggregate, so it can be traversed with foreach like a regular array.
Since PHP 5.5, password_hash() automatically generates a cryptographically secure salt, and passing a salt option is deprecated.
PASSWORD_DEFAULT currently points to bcrypt (password_hash), not md5, which is not used for password hashing in PHP 8.
password_verify correctly checks the plaintext password against the hash, which embeds its own random salt, so it returns true.
strip_tags() only removes HTML and PHP tags; SQL injection is prevented with prepared statements or proper escaping functions.
Calling session_regenerate_id() after login generates a new session ID, preventing attackers from using a pre-set session ID (session fixation).
php_sapi_name() returns a string describing the Server API, such as 'cli', 'fpm-fcgi', or 'apache2handler'.
session_destroy() removes server-side session data, but the client's session cookie remains until it is removed manually or expires.
Session data is only loaded into $_SESSION after session_start() is called; without it, $_SESSION is not populated.
array_find() was added in PHP 8.4, returning the first element of an array that satisfies a callback.
Property hooks were introduced in PHP 8.4, allowing get/set logic directly in property declarations.
PHP 8.4 introduced asymmetric visibility, allowing independent read and write scopes like public private(set).
The #[\NoDiscard] attribute was introduced in PHP 8.5 to mark functions whose return values should not be ignored.
The pipe operator |> was accepted and introduced in PHP 8.5, allowing values to be passed through a chain of callables.
The clone-with syntax (clone $obj with ['x' => 1]) was introduced in PHP 8.4.
array_first() and array_last() were introduced in PHP 8.5 as helpers to retrieve the first and last elements of an array.
The Partial Function Application v2 RFC was adopted for PHP 8.5, which shipped in November 2025.
The clamp_v2 RFC was accepted and the clamp() function was implemented in PHP 8.4.
The Context Managers v2 RFC was still in discussion/voting stages and had not been adopted into PHP as of that date.
The generics RFC was declined earlier (its vote concluded in late 2024), not in 2026.
No RFC to enable ZTS (multithreading) by default has been accepted in PHP; PHP continues to ship as a non-thread-safe build by default.
PHP 8.5 does not include generics; parameterized types remain unimplemented in the language.
PHP 8.5 became the latest stable release in November 2025, and PHP 8.6's GA is scheduled for November 19, 2026, after the given date.
PHP 6 was abandoned due to failed Unicode efforts, so PHP 5.6 was followed directly by PHP 7.0.
The RFC to add the #[\Deprecated] attribute was adopted and implemented in PHP 8.4.
In clean and onion architecture, dependencies always point inward, so inner layers (domain/core) have no knowledge of outer layers (infrastructure, UI).
In clean/domain-driven design, domain entities stay framework- and persistence-agnostic, depending only on PHP itself and the standard library.
Controllers and Twig templates belong to the delivery/presentation layer; business logic lives in use cases (and domain), which the controllers merely call.
In onion architecture, the innermost layer is the domain model (entities/business objects), with everything else wrapped around it.
Tools like deptrac statically analyze dependencies between layers and fail the build when forbidden calls are detected.

A use case (interactor) should be framework- and delivery-mechanism-agnostic, accepting only plain domain/DTO arguments, so it remains decoupled from HTTP details and infrastructure like an EntityManager.
In Domain-Driven Design, a Repository provides a collection-like interface for accessing aggregates/entities while encapsulating the underlying storage mechanism.
In clean architecture, database access is an infrastructure detail in the outer layer, so the domain and use case layers remain independent of the specific database technology.
In Domain-Driven Design, an aggregate is a cluster of domain objects treated as a single consistency unit with a root entity, not merely a database table.
By definition, a Value Object is immutable and two instances are considered equal when their field values match, regardless of identity.
In Domain-Driven Design, the aggregate root is the only member of an aggregate that external code may access to make changes.
In Domain-Driven Design, repositories are defined per aggregate root, since only aggregates are loaded and persisted as whole units.
Ubiquitous language, a core Domain-Driven Design concept, is the common vocabulary shared by developers and domain experts, used consistently in code, documentation, and conversation.
In Domain-Driven Design, a bounded context is the boundary within which a model and its ubiquitous language are consistent, while the same terms outside may refer to different models.
DDD recommends a rich domain model where entities contain behavior and business logic, making the anemic model generally considered an anti-pattern in DDD.
A bounded context defines an explicit boundary within which a particular model applies, so the same concept (e.g., 'Customer') may be represented by different classes in different contexts.
Symfony DI container instantiates services only when they are actually requested (e.g., via get() or injection into another service), not when the container itself is built.
The Symfony console command `php bin/console debug:router` lists all registered routes.
Symfony autowiring automatically discovers and injects services in src/, so you do not need to manually declare every service in services.yaml.
Twig compiles templates into PHP classes which are cached so they are only compiled once.
In dev, Symfony tracks container resources (config files, classes, etc.) and only recompiles the DI container when one of those tracked files changes.
Symfony reads the APP_ENV environment variable to determine whether it runs in dev, prod, or another environment.
Symfony controller methods must be public, since the framework invokes them from outside the class; private/protected methods cannot be routed.
Event subscribers do not receive events before listeners by default; both are dispatched according to their priority values, which can be defined for subscribers and listeners alike.
Symfony 6.0 removed the Guard authenticator system, making AuthenticatorInterface-based authenticators the only supported authentication mechanism.
The #[IsGranted(...)] attribute (e.g. #[IsGranted('ROLE_ADMIN')]) on a controller method denies access with a 403 when the role/permission check fails.
Symfony voters are custom authorization classes that decide whether access should be granted for a given attribute and subject object, called via isGranted('EDIT', $post).
Symfony 7 removed support for Doctrine-style doc-comment annotations, so validation constraints must be declared as PHP attributes (#[Assert\NotBlank]).
Symfony forms include CSRF protection by default, automatically generating and validating the CSRF token when the form is submitted.
Symfony form validation is performed server-side on submission, independent of any client-side HTML5 validation that may have passed.
Symfony's maker bundle command `make:form` generates a form class (FormType).
Symfony stores only the user's roles and identifier (like username) in the session token, never the plain-text password, since credentials are erased after authentication.
Symfony stores bundle configuration as separate files in config/packages, typically one file per bundle or topic (e.g., framework.yaml, twig.yaml).
This follows the standard dotenv convention (e.g., in Symfony): .env contains committed dev defaults, while .env.local holds real secrets and is excluded via .gitignore.
Symfony's console command `php bin/console debug:container` lists all registered services and their aliases in the service container.
Once the container is compiled and frozen (as in normal runtime), calling setParameter() throws a LogicException, so it cannot be used from a controller.
Since Symfony 3.4/4.0, services are private by default and can only be injected (or aliased), not fetched directly from the container.
Bundles work out of the box with sensible defaults; configuration in config/packages is optional and only needed to override or customize defaults.
In Symfony, environment variables are referenced in services.yaml using the %env(VAR)% syntax.
Symfony uses the APP_DEBUG environment variable (typically set to 1) to enable debug mode, which activates the profiler and Twig debugging.
Symfony Messenger supports multiple handlers for a single message by default; it can route one message to several handlers.
The sync transport handles the message immediately in the same process, bypassing the queue entirely, unlike async which queues it for a worker.
Symfony Messenger workers are started with the `php bin/console messenger:consume` console command.
In Symfony Messenger, the retry_strategy option is defined inside each transport's configuration under framework.messenger.transports, so failures can be retried differently per transport.
By default, Symfony Messenger uses the PhpSerializer (PHP's serialize function); JSON serialization requires configuring the Symfony Serializer transport serializer.
Symfony's Scheduler component schedules recurring messages and dispatches them through Messenger buses and transports.
The Doctrine Messenger transport (doctrine://default) stores queued messages in the messenger_messages database table via Doctrine.
Symfony Messenger lets you configure the middleware stack by appending or prepending your own custom middleware around the built-in ones.
Symfony follows a fixed schedule with major releases every two years and minor releases every six months, in May and November.
Symfony 8 requires PHP 8.4 or higher.
Symfony 7.0 removed support for docblock annotations, requiring PHP native attributes instead for validation, routes, and other features.
Symfony's AssetMapper serves CSS/JS files directly from imports without needing Node.js or webpack, configured via importmap.php.
Symfony 6.4 is an LTS (Long-Term Support) release, supported with bug fixes until November 2026 and security fixes until November 2027.
Symfony removes all deprecations from the previous major version's branch when a new major release comes out, so deprecated features stop working in the new major version.
Symfony ships an UPGRADE file (e.g., UPGRADE-7.0) with each major release describing all breaking changes and how to migrate.
The Symfony AssetMapper component serves JavaScript/CSS assets and manages importmaps without needing Node.js or Webpack.
Symfony 8.2 follows the regular May/November release schedule and would be released in late November 2026, after November 7.
Symfony follows a six-month release cycle, and with Symfony 8.1 released in May 2026, version 8.2 is scheduled for November 2026.
Symfony follows a predictable release cycle, so the version after 8.1 is 8.2.
In Symfony's release scheme, only x.0 versions are major releases; x.2 (like 8.2) is a minor release that is fully backward compatible and requires no rewrite.
PHP's release policy keeps backward compatibility within a major version, so updating from one minor version to another (e.g., 8.1 to 8.2) should not require code changes.
Following Symfony's release cycle (like 6.4 before 7.0), version 8.4 is the final minor release of the 8.x branch before Symfony 9.0.
Symfony 8.x is not expected to require PHP 8.5; new Symfony majors typically adopt a minimum PHP version around two versions old, not the very latest release.
Symfony's policy guarantees that code marked deprecated in a minor release series (like 8.x) is kept working until the next major release (9.0).
Twig is sandboxed and only allows registered filters, functions, and methods, not arbitrary PHP code.
Twig enables output auto-escaping (with the html strategy) by default, so printed variables are automatically escaped unless autoescape is disabled.
The |e filter escapes a string for safe output, and by default it uses the 'html' escaping strategy.
The twig/intl-extra package provides the format_number filter, which formats a number according to a given locale (e.g. {{ 1000 | format_number(locale='fr') }}).
In Twig, the |raw filter marks a value as safe, so the auto-escaper will not escape it.
In Twig, {{ }} outputs the value of an expression, while {% %} executes statements like if, for, and set.
Twig allows declaring variables inside a template using the {% set %} tag.
The dump() Twig function outputs the debug structure of a variable when the debug mode is enabled.
Bootstrap provides prebuilt CSS styles and JS components for styling pages, whereas SPA frameworks like Angular, React, or Vue manage application structure and routing.
The .container class provides a responsive fixed-width container that changes its max-width at each breakpoint.
Bootstrap's grid uses 12 columns per row, not 16 (though older versions were indeed built on CSS floats).
Bootstrap defines six breakpoints, but xs needs no infix, so the class-name infixes are sm, md, lg, xl, and xxl — five in total.
Bootstrap's spacing utilities multiply the $spacer variable (default 1rem), so .mt-3 equals 3 × $spacer.
Bootstrap 5 uses data-bs-toggle (e.g. data-bs-toggle="dropdown") to activate interactive components.
Bootstrap 5 removed the jQuery dependency entirely and uses vanilla JavaScript for all its components.
Bootstrap 5.3 dark mode is enabled with the data-bs-theme="dark" attribute on the root element, not a .dark class.
Doctrine ORM requires you to create the schema explicitly using tools like the SchemaTool or migrations; it never creates tables automatically when an entity is used at runtime.
EntityManager::persist() schedules a new entity for management, with SQL executed only at flush().
EntityManager::merge() was removed in Doctrine ORM 3 (after being deprecated in 2.x), so it no longer exists.
DQL (Doctrine Query Language) is object-oriented and operates on entities, their relationships, and fields rather than database tables and columns.
Doctrine's find() returns null when no entity matches the given identifier.
DoctrineBundle does not automatically call flush(); you must call it explicitly on the EntityManager to persist changes.
Doctrine's Unit of Work tracks managed entities, so changes are detected and flushed via flush() without calling persist() again.
Doctrine's remove() only marks the entity for deletion; the DELETE query is executed when flush() is called.
PostgreSQL's MVCC allows readers and writers to operate concurrently without blocking each other.
The EXPLAIN command prefixes a query to show its execution plan without actually running it.

SERIAL creates a column with a DEFAULT nextval() on a linked sequence, while GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY is the SQL-standard identity mechanism, which restricts accidental inserts and better ties the sequence's ownership to the column.
PostgreSQL treats NULLs as distinct from each other, so a UNIQUE constraint allows multiple rows with NULL in the column.
PostgreSQL's string_agg(expression, separator) aggregate concatenates string values with a specified separator.
Plain VACUUM only marks dead tuple space as reusable within the table files; only VACUUM FULL returns space to the operating system.
The PARTITION BY clause divides rows into groups over which the window function is computed.
READ COMMITTED only prevents dirty reads; each new read can see committed changes from other transactions, so non-repeatable reads can still occur.
PostgreSQL runs each statement in its own implicit transaction unless an explicit transaction (BEGIN/COMMIT) is opened.
The COMMIT command ends a transaction and permanently saves all its changes.
Indexes speed up any query that searches by the indexed column, including UPDATE and DELETE statements' WHERE clauses, not just SELECT.
PostgreSQL supports SAVEPOINT (with ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT) to roll back part of a transaction without aborting the whole transaction.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query to show real timing and row counts, while plain EXPLAIN only shows the plan without running it.
The pgvector extension provides vector data types and indexes (like HNSW and IVFFlat) for similarity search on embeddings in PostgreSQL.
A partial index is defined with a WHERE clause and indexes only the rows that satisfy that condition, making it smaller and faster for matching queries.
PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE level uses predicate-based conflict detection (SSI), not read-row locking.
HTTP 201 is the 'Created' status code, indicating the request successfully resulted in a new resource being created.
HTTP 204 No Content indicates a successful request with no response body, commonly returned after DELETE.
HTTP methods like DELETE, PUT, and GET are defined as idempotent, meaning repeated identical requests have the same effect as a single request.
Access-Control-Allow-Origin is a response header sent by the server to indicate which origins are permitted, not by the client.
HTTP status 429 Too Many Requests indicates the client has sent too many requests in a given time, exceeding a rate limit.
It's reversed: 4xx codes indicate client errors, while 5xx codes indicate server-side errors.
The Content-Type header indicates the MIME type of the body in both requests and responses.
RFC 5789 explicitly states PATCH is not required to be idempotent, whereas PUT is idempotent by HTTP semantics.
String comparison with == is not timing-safe and can behave unexpectedly, so password_verify() (or hash_equals()) should be used instead.
CSRF protection works by generating a random token per session that the server embeds in forms and verifies on state-changing requests to ensure the request originates from the site itself.
The CSP policy is delivered via the Content-Security-Policy HTTP response header (also historically X-Content-Security-Policy).
OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework that grants access to resources, not an authentication protocol; access tokens do not identify the user (that's the role of OpenID Connect).
XSS is prevented by escaping/encoding output in the correct context (e.g., HTML, attribute, JS), since validating input alone doesn't guarantee safe rendering.
In the authorization code flow, the authorization server redirects back to the redirect_uri with a 'code' parameter, which the client exchanges for an access token.
Refresh tokens have a longer lifetime and can be exchanged for new access tokens without requiring the user to re-authenticate.
A salt does not need to be secret—it is typically stored alongside the hash and used openly during verification; its purpose is to prevent precomputed rainbow-table attacks, not to hide the hash.
PHPUnit only recognizes classes that extend PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase as runnable tests.
setUp() runs before each individual test method; setUpBeforeClass() is the method that runs once before all tests in the class.
A data provider supplies multiple sets of arguments, so the test runs once for each data set it returns.
The expectException() method on PHPUnit's TestCase declares that the test expects an exception of the given class to be thrown.
In PHPUnit, it's the opposite: a stub is used only to return canned data, while a mock additionally verifies which methods were called (and with what arguments).
In PHPUnit 10, metadata moved from doc-comment annotations to native PHP attributes, so #[DataProvider] is recommended while @dataProvider is deprecated.
PHPUnit supports test dependencies via the @depends annotation, allowing a test to receive the result of a test it depends on.
PHPUnit randomizes test execution order with the --order-by=random command-line option.
